\chapter{Your First Verb, and the Form That Means I}
\label{ch:first-verb}
\hlchaptermodality{15}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what I do, in one word, with no pronoun at all.}

One word, one whole sentence — and why English cannot do the same.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hablar]{hablar — \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} which used to mean \textquotedblleft{}to tell tales\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C06-hablar}



\begin{quote}
Fixed phrases got you this far. \textbf{Hablar} (\textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}) is the first verb you will take apart and put back together. Today: the word itself. Next lesson: one ending, and it becomes about you.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{silent-h} — the \textbf{h is completely silent}: \emph{hablar} = \emph{ah-BLAR}. (Spanish \emph{h} never makes a sound.)
  \item \texttt{v-b} — the \emph{b} is a soft \emph{b}; \emph{hablo} = \emph{AH-bloh}.
\end{itemize}

That silent \emph{h} is not an accident of spelling. Latin's initial \textbf{f-} weakened in a whole set of Spanish words and eventually fell silent altogether, but the scribes kept writing a letter where it used to be — and that letter is \textbf{h}. You are looking at the gravestone of an \emph{f}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{hablar} comes from Latin \textbf{fābulārī}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to chat, to tell tales\textquotedblright{}} — from \textbf{fābula}, \textquotedblleft{}a story.\textquotedblright{} So \emph{to speak}, in Spanish, is at root \emph{to tell stories}. Notice Latin had a plainer verb available (\emph{loquī}, \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} which English keeps in \textbf{eloquent} and \textbf{loquacious}) — and Spanish chose the chattier, more colourful one.

That \textbf{fābula} is thoroughly English: \textbf{fable}, \textbf{fabulous} (\textquotedblleft{}story-like\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{confabulate}, and \textbf{ineffable} (\textquotedblleft{}un-speak-able\textquotedblright{}).

The single path you need today is \textbf{fābulārī $\to$ hablar}; later words will let you test how broadly that \emph{f- $\to$ h-} pattern reaches.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablar\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ah-BLAR}, silent \emph{h}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablar\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}fable, fabulous, ineffable\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{fābula} root
  \item the sound law — \textquotedblleft{}fābulārī\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}hablar\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word is \emph{hablar} from, and what English word shares it? (\emph{Fābulārī} $\leftarrow$ \emph{fābula} — \textbf{fable}.) What happened to its initial Latin \emph{f-}? (It weakened away, leaving the written but \textbf{silent} Spanish \emph{h-}.) Next: swap the \emph{-ar} for one letter, and \emph{hablar} becomes \emph{I speak}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hablo]{hablo — \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C06-hablo}



\begin{quote}
What is the word for \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Hablar}.) Say it once.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hablar — the verb, and the \emph{fābula} behind it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: change the ending, change who is speaking}]
\emph{Hablar} is the naming form — \textquotedblleft{}to speak.\textquotedblright{} It is not yet about anybody.

To make it about \textbf{you}, take off the \textbf{-ar} and put \textbf{-o} in its place:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{hablar} $\to$ \textbf{hablo} — \emph{I speak.}
\end{quote}

That is the whole operation. One ending, swapped.

And notice what you did not have to do: you did not add a word for \emph{I}. The \textbf{-o} is already carrying it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
The \textbf{-o} is old and it is nearly untouched. Latin marked \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} on a verb with \textbf{-ō}, a long \emph{o}: \emph{amō}, \textquotedblleft{}I love.\textquotedblright{} Two thousand years later Spanish still marks \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} with exactly that letter.

Most of Latin's endings wore down on the way to Spanish. This one did not. When you say \emph{hablo}, the last sound in your mouth is the same one a Roman used to say \emph{I}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Worth noticing.} English gave up. \emph{Speak} is \emph{speak} whoever is doing it, which is why English cannot let go of its pronouns. You will meet that difference properly in the very next lesson.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablo\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablo\textquotedblright{} again, and hear that the \emph{-o} is the part meaning \emph{I}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you turn \emph{hablar} into \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{}? (Drop \textbf{-ar}, add \textbf{-o}.) Which Latin ending is that \textbf{-o}? (\emph{-ō} — the same one.) Next: why \emph{hablo} is already a complete sentence.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hablo]{hablo — one word, one whole sentence}

\label{lesson:ES-C06-pro-drop}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{} in Spanish. (\emph{Hablo}.) Now count the words you said.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the pronoun you never needed}]
One word. And it is a complete, ordinary, grammatical Spanish sentence.

English needs two — \emph{I} and \emph{speak} — because English's ending is doing no work. Spanish needs one, because the \textbf{-o} already said \emph{I} in the previous lesson.

Spanish does have a word for \emph{I}. You will meet it. But putting it in front of \emph{hablo} is a little like saying \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I, I speak\textquotedblright{}} — the information is already there, and repeating it is something Spanish does only when it wants to make a point.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{The habit to build now.} When you want to say \emph{I speak}, say \textbf{hablo}. Not two words. One.
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
This is not Spanish being clever. It is English having lost something.

Old English marked its verbs properly — \emph{ic sprece}, \emph{þū sprecest}, \emph{hē spricþ}. Those endings were as distinct as Spanish's are. Then English wore them down until almost nothing was left: today \emph{speak, speak, speak, speak, speaks}. Four of the five are identical.

Once the endings stopped telling you who was speaking, the pronoun had to, and English could never put it down again.

Spanish kept its endings. So Spanish kept the choice.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablo\textquotedblright{} — one word, and stop there
  \item it as an answer to a real question, as if someone just asked whether you speak
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many words is \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{One} — \emph{hablo}.) What is the name for leaving the pronoun out? (\textbf{Pro-drop}.) Why can't English do it? (Its endings wore away, so only the pronoun is left to carry the person.) Next chapter: the same verb, aimed at somebody else.
\end{tcolorbox}
